input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

input.section_summary: Specify the evidence corpus interface, retrieval pipeline per section (query formulation, candidate pooling), ranking/scoring criteria, and the protocol for selecting and injecting top evidence into prompts. Cover caching and provenance tracking for each retrieved item.

output:
This section specifies the design and operational protocol of our per‑section evidence retrieval, indexing, and ranking pipeline. The description emphasizes reproducible, auditable artifacts (metadata, provenance records, and machine‑readable evidence attachments) rather than empirical claims about retrieval effectiveness. The procedures below reflect implementation choices used in our system; where relevant, we note these as design decisions rather than evaluated facts.

Corpus interface and indexing
- Corpus interface. The retrieval component exposes a stable programmatic API that supports (1) document-level metadata queries (document id, title, authors, year, source type), (2) passage‑level retrieval (document id, byte/character offsets, passage text), and (3) bibliographic export (bibtex or structured fields). The API returns both the raw document content and structured metadata for provenance recording.
- Indexing. Source documents are indexed at two granularities: (a) document‑level metadata and full‑text for coarse retrieval; and (b) passage‑level units (paragraphs or fixed‑length sliding windows) for fine‑grained retrieval and evidence extraction. Each index entry records its origin (document id and passage offsets) and the indexing timestamp to support reproducible retrieval runs.

Per‑section retrieval pipeline
- Query formulation. For each target section node, the system derives a retrieval query by combining: (i) the section title and its graph context (parent/child section headings and short summaries), (ii) any explicit claims or slot prompts from the section JSON schema (e.g., ``motivation'', ``dataset description''), and (iii) optional user‑supplied keywords. These elements are concatenated into a structured query template to preserve intent and scope for retrieval.
- Candidate pooling. The retrieval step returns a candidate pool from two complementary sources: (a) a lexical retrieval engine over the full‑text index (e.g., term‑based ranking) to capture exact matches and surface form overlaps; and (b) a semantic retrieval engine over vector embeddings of passages to capture paraphrased or semantically related evidence. The candidate pool is the union of top candidates from each engine, subject to de‑duplication by passage fingerprint.
- Passage normalization. Retrieved passages are normalized before ranking: whitespace and encoding normalized, author and section headers stripped or annotated, and a short excerpt (context window) extracted to present to the generator. Each normalized passage remains linked to its provenance record.

Ranking and scoring criteria
- Multi‑factor scoring. We rank candidate passages using a composite score that combines the retrieval engine score(s), a context relevance score (similarity between passage embedding and section query), and provenance quality signals (document recency, publication venue type, and presence of bibliographic metadata). This composite score is computed deterministically from the recorded signals so rankings are reproducible given the same index and query.
- Ordinal selection and thresholds. For prompt injection, the pipeline selects the top‑N passages by composite score. N is a configurable parameter per section type (for example, small for short ``limitations'' slots and larger for ``related work'') and treated as an implementation hyperparameter rather than an empirically tuned constant in this description.
- Diversity and de‑duplication. To reduce redundancy, the selection step enforces passage‑level diversity by filtering out passages whose normalized text exceeds a similarity threshold to any already selected passage. This yields a compact set of complementary evidence items for the generator.

Evidence injection and generator interface
- Structured evidence attachments. Each passage supplied to the generator is attached as a structured evidence object containing: passage text (excerpt), document id, passage offsets, retrieval scores, and bibliographic metadata. These attachments are rendered into the evidence‑aware prompt in a predictable template so that the generator can reference evidence items by index or explicit citation token.
- Prompt rules. Prompts instruct the generator to (a) use only the attached evidence items when producing factual claims that require citation, (b) include explicit inline citations linking claims to evidence indices or bibliographic keys, and (c) output the section in the required JSON schema with discrete fields for textual content and a citations list that enumerates the evidence object ids used.
- Mandatory citation constraint. The generator is required to annotate every non‑trivial factual sentence in the section body with at least one supporting evidence reference drawn from the attached evidence objects; the system treats the absence of such annotations as a validation failure to be handled by the repair procedures described in Section 3.3.

Caching, provenance, and reproducibility
- Deterministic retrieval snapshots. To support repeatable generation and downstream audits, the system snapshots the retrieval inputs and outputs for each section request: the structured query, index versions used, timestamps, returned candidate pool (with full metadata), and final selected evidence list. These records are stored alongside the section JSON output.
- Provenance fields. Every evidence object persisted with a section contains explicit provenance fields: document id, source filename or corpus id, passage offsets, retrieval scores from each engine, and the indexing timestamp. These fields allow auditors to re‑fetch the original passage or to re‑index and re-run the retrieval deterministically.
- Cache semantics. The pipeline maintains a content‑addressable cache keyed by (query, index version) to avoid unnecessary re‑retrieval and to ensure that repeated runs with identical inputs return identical candidate pools when the index has not changed.

Auditability and minimal‑trust assumptions
- Traceable claim→evidence links. Because evidence is attached and claims are annotated with evidence references in the JSON output, downstream auditors can map any generated assertion back to the exact passage(s) that were available to the model at generation time.
- Conservative defaults. Default system behavior favors requiring explicit evidence attachments for any factual claim and treating missing or low‑confidence provenance as a flag for human review; this is a pragmatic design choice to prioritize auditability over unconstrained recall in generation.

Limitations of this description
- The preceding protocol describes design and implementation choices of our retrieval and evidence injection pipeline. It does not report empirical retrieval effectiveness or evaluation results; those are presented in Section 4 and Section 5. Where quantitative tradeoffs (e.g., choice of N, similarity thresholds, or specific retrieval engines) are needed in practice, we treat them as tunable hyperparameters and report their settings and effects in the experimental sections rather than asserting unvalidated advantages here.
